The ROG Xbox Ally X is actually the best handheld on the market right now, by our estimation. That's in large part because its $1,000 price tag is actually very reasonable in the current, memory shortage-induced, price-inflated market. It helps that it's a decent handheld in its own right, especially thanks to its comfy grips and the new handheld Windows experience.

The ROG Xbox Ally X20 is almost the same, except it has some nice additions such as an OLED screen and TMR sticks, plus better thermals. The regular version is a fair bit cheaper, though, and would be getting my vote for that reason.

At any rate, it's great to see our fave handheld getting the option for this kind of performance boost in those games that need it. Oh, and Microsoft says Auto SR will be available for "select Windows Copilot+ PCs", too, though I'm not entirely sure what the selection criteria is.

#3673. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Is Set To Outsell The N64 Original In Its First Week

N64NintendoSwitch 2The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

If you pay close attention to the games industry you might have noticed that Nintendo released a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time last week. And if you went so far as to buy a copy of the Switch 2 release, you find yourself in the company of over five million others. The all-new version of the N64 classic has sold an extraordinary 5.2 million copies in its first four days on sale, bringing it extraordinary close to the original version’sÂ lifetime sales.

In 1998, the Nintendo 64 version ofÂ Ocarina of Time literally broke records, receiving the beer company’s accolade for most pre-orders of all time, at 325,000. In its first week it sold a million copies, reaching 2.5 million by three weeks. It was only outsold that year byÂ GoldenEye, and two years later had sold a mighty 7.6 million copies worldwide. All very impressive stuff. And then the Switch 2 remake suggests it hold its pint of Guinness.

Nintendo has announced that theÂ Ocarina remake sold 5.2 million copies worldwide in just its first four days, making it the best-selling Switch 2 game across that timespan so far. It also means it’s sold 70 percent as many copies as the original ever did, in 0.5 percent of the time. Crikey. With three more days to go before its first week on sale is up, it seems pretty likely that it’ll match the N64 version’s sales in time for the weekend.

Nintendo’s figures include both digital and physical copies, making them more accurate than the somewhat guestimated numbers from tracking companies and chart compilers, and Nintendo suggests 5.2 million is rounding down.

You might assume that these modern figures are largely driven by the huge growth in the total gaming market in 2026 when compared with 1998. I sure did. But digging into the numbers it ends up looking even more impressive. The N64 was two years old by the time Ocarina was released, and that console sold a total of 32.93 million units across its entire lifetime. The Switch 2 after a year-and-a-half has sold 26.35 million units. While there are no official numbers on how many of those N64s had sold by November 1998, it’s reasonable to assume the numbers weren’t wildly different. In that light, the Switch 2Â Ocarina sales are all the more stunning, and also speak to a very different audience attitude to the release of new games, with far bigger up-front spikes and more diminishing tails.

Either way, there’s money in them their Hyrulean hills, and this will only drive Nintendo further to remake all those classicÂ Zelda titles, and hopefully use the newÂ Ocarina art and engine to craft something new.

#3672. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

90 Day: Hunt For Love surprised me when two cast members decided to give dating a serious go, but I'm not expecting it to last. Sorry to Jamal Menzies and Emma Perry, but I'm already seeing all the red flags that this trial-run relationship could be over by the time we reach the Season 2 tell-all.

Emma continues to be the best part of Season 2 as episodes continue to air as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Her continued feud with Chloe Fabiano and relationship with Jamal have carried this season, but I don't know if there's more to the latter than just providing 90 Day Fiancé fans with some quality entertainment.

From storming off in the middle of arguments to sitting down for therapy sessions, it feels like Emma and Jamal are already preparing for an appearance on 90 Day: The Last Resort. These are the arguments I'd expect from a couple who were married and on the verge of splitting, not a couple who only just decided to start dating.

Emma insisted the drama in the latest episode was tied to her ongoing feud with Chloe, and that outside of the show, she and Jamal wouldn't have as many problems. Based on both of their past storylines, I'm more apt to believe they're just very quick to feel deep emotions, which can be a volatile combo when two people are in a relationship.

Imagine my surprise when I saw an update from 90 Day Fiancé insider Shabooty suggesting Jamal and Emma are still together. A photo apparently taken earlier this year is making the rounds online, and it shows them vacationing together in Aruba.

90 Day: Hunt For Love Has Me Wondering If Brittany Intentionally Sabotaged Michael's Love Life

All this to say, neither is posting clues that they're still together as of writing. It's possible the trip to Aruba was something for them to see if they wanted to keep dating after Hunt For Love and that we'll see that unfold in a future spinoff.

If Jamal and Emma are together, I'd genuinely be curious to see how it's going. On the off chance they are going strong, they may just turn into one of the all-star couples of 90 Day Fiancé. I'm rooting for this franchise to have a new star couple, so that would be an upside of these two getting together.

We'll get some updates when the tell-all hits, but until then, we'll just have to keep watching 90 Day: Hunt For Love. Season 2 is so much better than the previous season so far, so here's hoping a potential third season is even better.

So, uhhh, apparently the long-rumoured 24 GB version of the RTX 5080 will not be coming to fruition, contrary to the previous rumour we reported on, which itself was contrary to previous rumours, which were contrary to pre– you get the idea. This latest one is a rumour, too, courtesy of Gazlog on X and made visible to us via the pretty reputable leaker Harukaze. The latter puts it clearly: "RTX 5080 24GB IS DROPPED."

Funnily enough, if plans for this GPU have indeed been dropped, I'm actually taking it as a win. That's because the previous word on the grapevine was that it would not be an additional GPU, but a replacement for the RTX 5090 and the regular 16 GB version of the RTX 5080.

In other words, gamers looking for a high-end GPU would almost certainly have to splash out even more cash than they already do to get their hands on one, or settle for an RTX 5070 Ti. With GPU prices being what they are already, that would be far from welcome news.

Given all this, what corroborates the latest rumour that the RTX 5080 24 GB is dropped is the fact that Nvidia has explicitly said that the RTX 5090 is not dead. That's according to Nvidia GeForce SVP Jeff Fisher:

"Although there are other variants of the RTX 5090 (chip), production has not been discontinued, and Nvidia will continue to ship, which is very important."

With the RTX 5090 still live, it makes less sense to release an RTX 5080 24 GB. Less likely, but still possible, given Nvidia could cancel the RTX 5080 16 GB and have a 24 GB version even with an RTX 5090 still in the lineup. With the RTX 5090 currently being hard to find in stock anyway, and ridiculously expensive when you do find it, there would still be room for a 24 GB RTX 5080, aimed primarily at AI workloads.

#3669. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3666. Amy Poehler And Steve Carell Bonded Over How Poorly The Office And Parks And Rec Went Their First Seasons

If Parks and Recreation and The Office have one thing in common, it's that both series took a little while to find their footing. Of course, these two comedies have more than one thing in common -- both aired on NBC around the same time, both were created (or co-created in Parks & Rec's case, alongside Michael Schur) by Greg Daniels, and both debuted with big expectations from fans of an existing series. It's no surprise that Amy Poehler would find some very common ground with Steve Carell when talking about their experiences on their respective shows.

Not all of the best sitcoms of all time got off to an amazing start. The Office and Parks and Recreation are two perfect examples of shows that needed more than a few episodes to find their groove. In March, back when Steve Carell's new HBO series Rooster was just getting started, the Office star sat down with Amy Poehler on her Good Hang podcast. Among the topics that came up was how poorly their earlier sitcoms were initially received by viewers.

As Poehler tells it, there are two people that she's been told she's a "poor man's version of," and Carell is one of them. She went on to laugh about how terribly the debut of Parks and Recreation went, saying:

Parks and Rec had the worst launch ever. Everyone was like, 'This is not The Office, we don't like this.' I just remembered we're like -- 'You're not Steve and you're not -- we don't like it!' And I think I just dissociated and was like, 'well.'"

That viewers might have been looking for more of what they'd come to know and love from The Office -- and Carell's character, Michael Scott -- is not that surprising, given its creators and the fact that it was another single-camera mockumentary-style workplace comedy. In the case of Parks and Rec, the focus was on the office workers at the Parks and Recreation department of a small town in Indiana. That included Poehler's optimistic and determined Leslie Knope.

When Greg Daniels and Michael Schur's new series debuted in spring of 2009, it was around the same time that The Office was wrapping up its fifth season. Months prior to Parks and Rec's debut, The Office had its post-Super Bowl double episode, "Stress Relief," which was watched by millions (and is remembered as one of the best episodes of the series). The Office was firmly established with its fanbase, while Parks and Rec was just getting warmed up.

It's almost easy to forget that The Office had faced a similar challenge years earlier, as Carell noted in his conversation with Poehler:

Our pilot was the lowest casting pilot in the history, I think, of NBC. People really hated it ... They actively hated this show, and I don't quite know how it got legs after that.

Lest we not forget, The Office didn't debut to universal praise and sky-high ratings when it arrived in 2005, and it was nearly cancelled after its first season. The show arrived on the heels of the success of the 2001 Ricky Gervais sitcom that started it all, and to say that the U.S. version of the beloved UK comedy had big shoes to fill would be an understatement.

Personally, I didn't hate the first season of the U.S. version of The Office when it aired, but I also wouldn't argue with many of the criticisms of the show's first six episodes. That's a whole other conversation though. Getting back to the topic at hand, in his conversation with Amy Poehler, Carell called himself out as "a poor man's Ricky Gervais."

I don't think anyone would say that about Carell today, but he certainly had a high bar to meet when leading the U.S. version of The Office. And from what he said, he intentionally didn't watch more than a minute of Gervais in Office:

I watched like a minute of him, and he was so good, and so specific, and so funny, I thought, if I watch a second more, I'm just going to go on an audition with that. I won't be able to even imagine it a different way.

There really is only one David Brent, so it's understandable that Carell wouldn't want to try to recreate that character in Michael Scott. Ultimately, Carell's character became iconic in his own right, thanks in large part to the actor's comedic brilliance. Several seasons after he made his debut as Michael Scott, Carell had a say in how his character would exit the series.

All of this to say, I can see why Carell and Poehler would connect on this particular topic, as both of them saw success in their respective roles and shows, but it wasn't instant and both had to find their way out from under the shadow of other performances. Each show had to find their own way to success, and it's just really fortunate that both were given time and seasons to do so. I can't imagine a TV world without Michael Scott or Leslie Knope!

You can watch Parks and Recreation and The Office streaming with a Peacock subscription.

#3665. Pete Hegseth Responds to JD Vance Blaming Midterms Loss on Iran War

Pete Hegseth is responding to Vice President JD Vance’s claim the GOP suffered major losses in the 2026 midterm elections because of the wildly-unpopular Iran war.

“I respect the vice president greatly, and I’m certainly not going to exchange in any finger-pointing, and thankfully, politics is not really my thing,” Hegseth, a former Fox News weekend political news host, said in a press briefing on Tuesday, November 10, via NBC News. “I do the Department of War and making sure we’re prepared and ready.”

The United States Secretary of Defense, 46, continued, “A lot of people are going to look at the conflict and assess it, and the vice president has been a critical member of the team in every aspect of this, and we’re grateful for all the input he’s given me personally and our department.”

Earlier this month, Vance, 42, shared his personal — and lengthy — assessment on why the majority of Americans voted for Democrats in various midterm races, resulting in the Democratic party regaining control of the House and the Senate while flipping historically-red states like Texas, Kansas and more.

After allegedly analyzing data and speaking with pollsters, the vice president came to the conclusion that “the reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote via X on November 4. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

In his first press briefing at the Pentagon in nearly 190 days, Hegseth said he was focused on the future and keeping Americans safe amid a bipartisan push to remove him from his position.

“Going forward, we’re going to learn all those lessons and apply them,” he shared. “But I agree with what the president said when he said, ‘Hey, if I had to do this all over again, would we do it again? Absolutely.’”

Hegseth’s latest comments come just one day after Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) unveiled eight articles of impeachment against him.

Massie, 55, accuses President Donald Trump’s cabinet member of violating the U.S. Constitution and other laws during U.S. military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

“Some argue Hegseth has been effective,” Massie wrote via X on Tuesday, November 10. “I would agree. He’s been effective at breaking the law and violating the Constitution.”

In a press briefing, Hegseth called impeachment attempts a “farce” and “stunt.”

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability,” he claimed. “It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man’s final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president, to this country and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it.”

#3664. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is nearing its 20-year anniversary, and many fans have been watching the Marvel movies in order since Day 1. The shared universe (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription) has a few fan favorite franchises, chief among them being James Gunn's Guardians of the Galaxy. I've been missing Nebula and the rest of the team, but Karen Gillan recently gave me some hope about their return.

The end of Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 saw the team splitting up and going their separate ways. The final title card confirmed that Chris Pratt's Star-Lord would return to the MCU eventually, which put doubt into whether or not we'd ever see everyone else. In an interview with The Direct, Gillan was asked if there's a chance we'll see Nebula back in upcoming Marvel movies, with the actress responding with:

Maybe... You know I can't tell you that [laughs]. I have Marvel snipers on me. I have definitely spoken to them. Whether or not that was about making another appearance or not is a different story. Okay, waffle without saying anything at all. I'm still going. Basically, no spoilers over here.

Honestly, I'll take it. This isn't a confirmation about if/when we'll see the Blue Meanie back in the shared universe, but the fact that Karen Gillan is in contact with the powers that be at Marvel is a hopeful message. Nebula is one of my favorite characters in the entire MCU, and I'd love any opportunity to catch up with her sometime in the future.

When we last saw Nebula, she and Drax were committed to staying on Knowhere and raising the children that they saved from the villainous High Evolutionary. I'd love to se how this was going, as well as how Karen Gillan's character stands with her the revived Gamora. There are certainly narrative threads to pull from, so let's hope that the studio moves forward with a project that includes Nebula.

James Gunn is departing as co-CEO of DC Studios, which might offer some hope for Guardians of the Galaxy fans who want to see more from the cosmic team of heroes. Now that his schedule is freed up, perhaps he'll be inspired enough to explore what happened after Vol. 3. After all, Marvel fans adore the Guardians.

For now fans can re-watch Karen Gillan's tenure as Nebula on Disney+. That includes the three Guardians movies, the Holiday Special, as well as appearances in Avengers: Infinity War, Endgame, and Thor: Love and Thunder.

The next MCU movie hitting theaters is Avengers: Doomsday on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll just have to see if the Guardians of the Galaxy end up popping up in that movie or its sequel Secret Wars.

One thing I’ve learned from spending my days shopping for a living? You definitely don’t need a designer budget to dress like you have one. In fact, some of the prettiest blouses I’ve come across lately are hiding on Amazon, and they look like they belong in the window of a chic little boutique.

I rounded up 13 of my favorite finds that have all the details I typically associate with much pricier pieces, from romantic ruffles and delicate embroidery to flattering silhouettes and rich fall colors. Think feminine gingham tops, elegant button-downs and flowy blouses that make getting dressed feel a little more fun. The best part is that every single one costs less than $30!

1. My Favorite: Fall is the perfect time to swap basic button-downs for something with a little more character. This brown gingham blouse features romantic ruffle detailing, a softly gathered neckline and voluminous sleeves that make it feel effortlessly chic. The earthy color palette also pairs beautifully with everything from cream trousers to dark denim and suede accessories.

2. Burgundy Beauty: Deep jewel tones always make their way back into my wardrobe once the temperatures start dropping, and this burgundy blouse is a perfect example of why. The rich color looks especially striking against the gold statement buttons, while the gently puffed sleeves add a feminine touch. Pair it with cream trousers and gold jewelry for a polished look that works well beyond the office.

3. Olive Obsession: Olive green is one of those underrated fall colors that somehow works with almost everything in my closet. This floral lace blouse makes the shade even prettier with its oversized embroidered flowers, delicate eyelet cutouts and softly gathered sleeves. A reviewer even compared it to something “you’d find in a boutique,” which speaks to its elevated appearance.

4. Make a Statement: Sometimes all an outfit needs is one eye-catching piece, and this floral chiffon blouse certainly delivers. Its rich rust-colored print, voluminous sleeves and softly ruffled neckline give it plenty of personality without sacrificing versatility. I especially love how the loose-fitting silhouette offers a little extra room through the midsection.

5. Brown Sugar: Chocolate-brown tones are everywhere this fall, but I love how this printed blouse gives the color trend a softer, more artistic spin. Its oversized abstract pattern, gold-tone buttons and voluminous sleeves create a beautiful balance of playful and polished. The neutral palette also makes it surprisingly easy to incorporate into an existing wardrobe.

6. Darling Denim: Who says denim shirts have to be rugged or oversized? This puff-sleeve denim blouse puts a feminine spin on the wardrobe staple with its ruffled neckline, button-front detailing and softly gathered shoulders. I especially love that it comes in everything from classic blue and light-wash denim to darker blue, black and gray options.

7. Bow Beautiful: Some blouses are all about the front, but this bow-back beauty is just as charming from behind. The oversized bow adds a romantic surprise, while the ruffled shoulders, square neckline and flowy fit make it equally pretty from the front. I especially love the warm rust-orange shade for fall, though it also comes in several other colors.

8. Boho Beauty: I’m always drawn to blouses that have a relaxed, bohemian feel without looking too casual. This lace-trimmed top combines delicate Swiss-dot fabric, intricate embroidery and romantic ruffled cuffs for a beautifully feminine finish. I also love the creamy apricot shade, which makes it a versatile piece to wear throughout fall and winter.

9. Leaf It To Me: If I could pick one blouse to wear on repeat this fall, this leaf-embroidered top would be a serious contender. Between the rich rust-brown color, textured botanical detailing and romantic ruffled neckline, it practically belongs at a pumpkin patch or cozy weekend brunch. I’d throw it on with my favorite jeans and ankle boots for an outfit that feels festive without looking like I’m trying too hard.

10. Pretty Polka Dots: Something about chocolate brown and white polka dots feels so charming to me, especially during the cooler months. This printed long-sleeve blouse features delicate ruffle accents, a button-down front and softly gathered sleeves that make it feel both feminine and polished. I could see myself wearing it to a fall brunch, a dinner date or even Thanksgiving with the family.

11. Pleated Perfection: Some days I want to look polished, but the last thing I feel like wearing is a stiff, fitted button-down. That’s where this navy babydoll blouse comes in, with its breezy silhouette, softly gathered waist and feminine ruffled neckline. It also comes in several colors, including pink, teal, cream, black and green, if navy isn’t your favorite.

12. Waist-Defining: If there’s one thing I appreciate in a blouse, it’s a silhouette that does a little of the flattering work for me. This smocked peplum blouse cinches at the waist before flaring out over the stomach, creating a beautiful hourglass effect. I also love the muted green gingham print, which feels especially charming for fall coffee dates and weekend outings.

13. Stripe Appeal: If there’s one thing I can’t resist, it’s a classic wardrobe staple with a chic detail. This striped puff-sleeve blouse combines a timeless pinstripe pattern with dramatic sleeves and ruffled trim that make it feel so much more special than your average button-down. The soft apricot-and-white color combination also gives it a lighter, more feminine feel than traditional workwear.

#3661. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

There is a time-honored tradition of Saturday Night Live cast members and hosts “breaking” on the show, when they just can’t contain their laughter. It’s often some of the best moments of any episode, but it can really stress out cast members when it happens. Ashley Padilla recently opened up about it and how she reacted to a specific example of that happening to her while working in a sketch with host Ryan Gosling and fellow castmate Mikey Day.

In a recent interview, Padilla talks about how she writes sketches and thinks of them like a song, with beats to follow. If every sketch has a rhythm to follow, fellow actors going out of their way to make her laugh is like someone banging out of rhythm with a cowbell. It happened to Padilla in a sketch called “Cyclops” last season while Gosling was hosting (and it wasn't the only time in that episode). She talks about how it affected her and what goes through her head when it happens to her. Padilla told Time:

It depends because if someone is making you laugh, the laughter's coming from like, ‘What are you doing?’ I felt that in Cyclops. There was this like — Mikey Day [and] Ryan Gosling were just messing with me like two older brothers and I was laughing out of sheer — I couldn't believe what was happening. I was like, ‘How dare you guys. Stop it.’ They were making me laugh, you know?.... That was not planned.

In the sketch, you can see Padilla begging the two of them to stop, though they are clearly entertained enough to keep it going. Honestly, they pretty much abused her, though Day did (kind of) warn her about what they would be up to. Padilla explains:

Mikey said, ‘We might come at you once.’ I went, ‘OK, bring it on,’ you know? That, where I couldn’t get a word out, that was me begging. I have a cue card in front of me. I got to read this thing. I couldn’t believe [it]. I was laughing so hard. So that was because the audacity from these two was killing me.

I have to be honest here: the sketch is actually much funnier with Padilla trying as hard as she can not to lose it as Day and Gosling keep moving towards her, as she literally begs them to “stop.” I’m not sure the sketch would’ve been funny otherwise. Clearly Day and Gosling (plus Kenan Thompson) are having a blast hazing Padilla. They even cheer when it seems they got her to break. Lorne Michaels might not like it (though that might be a misconception), and the cast members get frustrated by it, but as a member of the audience, I love it.

Saturday Night Live Season 52 is well underway on the 2026 TV schedule, and cast members have been breaking for decades. Gosling himself broke in a previous hosting gig, so it’s not like it’s ever going to stop. I hope it never does anyway. Heck, I’d love to see it happen more often!

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3658. Patrick Mahomes and Wife Brittany Announce They're Expecting Baby No. 4

Patrick Mahomes and his wife, Brittany Mahomes, are ready to expand their team in 2027.

“Another blessing from God🥹🙏🏼,” the couple wrote via Instagram on Tuesday, November 10, when announcing they are expecting baby No. 4. “& then there were 6🤍.”

In the announcement, Patrick, 31, and Brittany’s kids Sterling, 5, Bronze, 3, and Golden, 22 months, gathered around mom and placed their hands on her belly as they posed for family photos by the beach.

The pregnancy news may come as a surprise to fans of the couple, who remember Brittany, 31, previously telling reporters that she wasn’t sure if more children were in her future.

“We’re done, we’re done for a while,” she said in a June 2025 episode of the “Whoops” podcast. “I don’t know. I mean, I feel like you can never say you’re done. I think three is all I need.”

At the same time, the Kansas City Current women’s soccer team coowner couldn’t hide her love and joy of being a parent.

“Being a mom changed so many things in my life and changed how I looked at so many things,” Brittany told Yahoo Entertainment in June. “It really reshaped and redefined a lot of things in my life.”

She continued, “It’s made me more intentional, more purposeful and, honestly, more motivated to keep going and keep showing my kids that there are no boundaries in front of you. You can achieve anything. You can be a part of anything that you want to. You need to dream big and understand that you have to work hard and do the hard things to do the fun things.”

While sports fans know Patrick as the Super Bowl champion quarterback of the Kansas City Chiefs, the NFL stud also previously shared how much he loves being a dad.

During a July 2023 episode of Netflix’s Quarterback docuseries, Patrick acknowledged that everybody sees the game days. Very few, however, get a look into life at home.

“They don’t see how you have to manage playing football and being a dad and being a husband,” he shared. “It’s football. You’re gonna have highs. You’re gonna have the lows. You put so much into this that you want to win, you want to succeed. And you want to win that Super Bowl at the end of the year. But I have to be a dad too. I have to be a husband.”

#3657. Susie Wiles Is Out. What Will Trump Do When He Runs Out of Women to Fire?

You know how after millions of people make clear that they despise not just your political project but also you personally, the logical response is to triple down on the specific things they hate?

That’s Donald Trump’s signature move. Three days after Democrats flipped seven Senate seats—nine if you feel bullish on Mississippi and Alaska—and secured a House majority, winning 253 seats and counting, the president announced that his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, would be replaced by Stephen Miller.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Even though polls indicating a blue wave proliferated before the election, this particular outcome still comes as a surprise. After all, Wiles had apparently proven her ability to ride out storms before—including everything that rocked Trump’s 2024 campaign, which Wiles managed, and her choice to sit for 10 interviews with Vanity Fair’s Chris Whipple in 2025, during which she discussed Elon Musk’s drug use and JD Vance’s true motives for embracing Trump. “Despite his travails, Trump needs Wiles and almost everyone around him knows it,” Whipple recently wrote in a follow-up story tracing rumors of Wiles’s imminent axing.

But now Wiles’s luck has finally run out. Why? Perhaps because she is, in the end, a woman.

Trump’s first term was marked by all sorts of chaos, including frequent arrivals to and departures from the White House. (Remember Omarosa?) But it doesn’t take Jessica Fletcher to detect that this time around, there’s a distinct pattern when it comes to whom Trump is willing to toss aside when the going gets rough. The scalps of the no-scalps era all have barrel curls. As Texas representative Jasmine Crockett observed in April, “He will throw the incompetent women under the bus a lot faster than the incompetent men.”

On March 5, following an uprising against the administration’s mass-deportation effort that culminated in two protesters being killed by ICE agents in Minnesota, Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem was axed. After wrath over the administration’s botched handling of the Epstein files, Attorney General Pam Bondi was fired in April.

Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Trump’s labor secretary, resigned later that month amid a misconduct investigation. Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence, who couldn’t sell Trump’s disastrous war with Iran, submitted her resignation in May, after her husband was diagnosed with cancer. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt stepped down—of her own accord—in August. Following an embarrassing Wall Street Journal investigation, Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece—and former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr.—was forced to resign last month.

Though you may have already forgotten all about her, Katie Zacharia had perhaps the least distinguished tenure of all: She gave her first briefing as Trump’s new press secretary on a Tuesday and was forced out by Friday of the same week. Shortly before Wiles’s ouster this week, Harmeet Dhillon, who helped kill DEI after joining the civil rights division of Trump’s Justice Department, announced she was stepping down.

All this, and Pete Hegseth still has a job.

What are we to make of the fact that Trump’s departed all happen to harbor two X chromosomes? Could it be, perhaps, that President “Grab ’Em by the Pussy” has a problem with women—even the loyalists who are largely responsible for helping him claw his way back into the White House in the first place? (Does Trump win, or even run, in 2024 without Wiles? It’s a possibility I’d like to see Rodham author Curtis Sittenfeld explore in an upcoming novel.)

The one thing we can be sure about is that, as of right now, there are only three women left in Trump’s 21-person Cabinet. The members of that trio—Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Kelly Loeffler, administrator of the Small Business Administration—might want to watch their blowout. (So should Natalie Harp.) Perhaps after they go, Trump will start employing the principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion while stabbing his allies in the back.

It's one of the most authentically queer movies I've ever seen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

2026 has been a solid year for movies, with smaller-budget movies like Obsession managing to make it big at the box office. There were also a number of daring new A24 movies, and that studio is offering another daring entry with Jordan Firstman's Club Kid. I was able to catch an early screening of the dramedy, which had me laughing and crying in equal measures throughout its brisk 121-minute runtime. Club Kid is my favorite movie of the entire year (so far), and I'm truly obsessed with its portrayal of gay nightlife.

Over the past few years, there's been a ton of conversation about the importance of LGBTQ+ representation in the media. While we got a steamy book-to-screen adaptation with Heated Rivalry, Club Kid offers an incredibly authentic look at nightlife in the community, warts and all. As a gay man in my mid-30s, I thought it was impressive how the depictions were, allowing me to relate intimately with this acclaimed new film.

Jordan Firstman is the writer, director and star of Club Kid, and deserves all the flowers he's received at festivals like Cannes and TIFF. While audiences might know him from his scene-stealing roles in English Teacher (streaming with a Hulu subscription) and Ms. Marvel, he takes center stage as protagonist Peter. He's a party promoter and habitual drug user who has been raging in the New York City nightlife scene for a decade, and is feeling the effects that his nocturnal proclivities take on him.

When Peter is fired from his job and arguably at his lowest, he's surprised to learn he has a son named Arlo (Reggie Absolom), the result of having sex with a woman in a darkroom years ago. What follows is a grittier take on Big Daddy, and we watch Peter and his son bond when he's suddenly dropped off at his door following the death of Arlo's mother.

Throughout the movie, we're shown an unapologetic and unfiltered look at the gay nightlife scene, including the drug use that can often accompany it. The movie's opening sequence shows Peter at the height of his career as a promoter. I was immediately struck by how real the club scene was, showing the various mini-conversations that happen in a crowded bar. Peter and his friends also engage in a mixture of drugs, especially GHB, ketamine and cocaine. It's when he's crossfaded that he eventually has sex with a woman, in a scene set in the venue's darkroom, where folks go to engage in anonymous sex.

Darkrooms have a long history in the LGBTQ+ community, and have been portrayed onscreen in projects like Harvey Fierstein's Torch Song Trilogy. While some audiences might balk at the scene in Club Kid, I have to applaud Firstman for showing them in such a real way, potentially educating straight moviegoers in the process.

Peter's relationship with drugs is also a major part of this movie, and I once again was shocked by how close to home it felt. I've seen firsthand how alluring and insidious drug use can be in nightlife, and have lost friends to it. Firstman's protagonist is given reason to change his lifestyle when he suddenly becomes a parent, but there are so many queer folks who are never able to separate themselves from the scene. While I've never had the experience of meeting a child I didn't know I had, I couldn't help but relate to the story told throughout the film.

Club Kid gets its wide theatrical release November 6th as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll have to see if another movie manages to beat it as my favorite movie of the year... but I doubt it. Now let Jordan Firstman direct whatever else he wants.

#3655. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3653. How the ‘Glee’ and ‘Girls’ Revivals Can Avoid Mistakes Made by Other TV Reboots

The blue-tinged afterglow of the 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both the House and Senate, unleashed a burst of online millennial optimism. Some have credited a pair of newly revived Obama-era coming of age TV shows that often got political themselves, Ryan Murphy’s Glee and Lena Dunham’s Girls, with being a precursor to the Blue Wave.

But for all of the internet’s excitement for new episodes of Glee and Girls , no one said aging beloved characters (who is Hannah Horvath at 40?), or addressing the current sociopolitical moment (will Sue Sylvester in a MAGA hat be inevitable?!) would come without risk. How do the Girls and Glee reboots meet nostalgic expectations while delivering something new and prescient about where the world is now? Perhaps Dunham and Murphy can draw lessons about aging gracefully in adaptation from revivals that have aired before them.

Ahead, a guide to do’s and don’ts for the return of generational TV, from the second coming of Sex and the City to Roseanne’s rocky renewal.

Riding a high from his Emmy-nominated shows including Ted Lasso and Shrinking (Apple TV), plus Rooster (HBO), series creator Bill Lawrence relaunched Scrubs, now airing its second season on ABC, into a post-Abbott Elementary landscape—where network TV craves workplace comedies for its airwaves. It seems that the folks behind Glee and Girls, respectively, have found the right moment to return to TV. Murphy has spoken about Glee’s recent streaming resurgence for younger audiences, and Dunham is coming off a headline-making book tour for her bestselling memoir Famesick, written about her time making Girls 1.0.

Rather than write themselves out of the show’s controversial final season, in which most of the show’s central cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, Sarah Chalke, were sidelined in favor of an entirely new group of characters, the creative team opted to retcon the entire ninth season and start fresh for the reboot. That means Glee can freely pretend its own flashforward—in which Rachel Berry is a surrogate mother for fellow Glee Club pals Kurt and Blaine could be abandoned. And maybe Shoshanna never decided she was too good for the rest of the Girls and they can all be dysfunctional friends again…right?

A political sketch titled “Oh Honey,” which reunited original cast members Debra Messing, Eric McCormack, Sean Hayes, and Megan Mullally in support of Hillary Clinton ahead of the 2016 presidential election, may not have prevented a Donald Trump presidency. But it did garner millions of views online, earning the attention of top NBC brass who hoped to capitalize on the nostalgia by relaunching Will & Grace in 2017. While the Glee Club has yet to release their own teaser, Dunham announced the Girls revival via four-way video call with cast members Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, and Zosia Mamet that promptly sent the internet into a tailspin.

While the Will & Grace revival lasted for three seasons largely because of its ability to engage with the day’s political issues, particularly as they related to the LGBTQ+ community, some felt the show became too steeped in Trumpland. In one episode, a Trump-supporting Karen even gets staunchly liberal Grace a job decorating his Oval Office. Girls and Glee will have to strike a similarly delicate balance with their own returns—incorporating the current political landscape in ways that feel natural to the narrative, as much as one can when often tone-deaf show choir kids and Brooklyn hipsters are involved.

Just as And Just Like That made a splash by murdering Mr. Big in the first episode via Peloton-induced heart attack, Glee and Girls should aim for maximum impact upon arrival. Maybe Adam Driver’s character meets his end while going method for a role and learning a dangerous new skill. As for Glee, perhaps the character played by Grammy-winning Finneas O’Connell (brother and music producer of Billie Eilish), could go up in a blaze of glory. Despite getting his start with a four-episode arc in the show’s final season, in 2020 O’Connell claimed that he’d never seen Glee, including the episodes he was in.

Taking a show outside of its comfort zone in the right ways raises the stakes—and highlights core tensions from the original series (see also: Miranda shown riding the subway for the first time). But some viewers felt And Just Like That… showrunner Michael Patrick King’s inclusion of diverse voices into the narrative veered too far outside of the shoebox with Che Diaz, the divisive podcast-cohost–slash-comedian–slash–veterinarian-office-worker that took the brunt of audience ire over freshly sober Miranda’s decision to divorce her husband Steve. New characters can become de facto villains for a series revival, particularly if they interfere with cherished dynamics from the show’s first run.

The return of Kelsey Grammer’s sitcom hero Frasier Crane was undercut by the absence of breakout supporting characters Niles and Daphne, as actors David Hyde Pierce and Jane Leeves did not reprise their roles for the reboot. Luckily, the core four of Girls have already signed on for their five-episode revival, and several Glee alums are in talks for its reboot, including series lead Lea Michele.

In addition to some of the creative challenges facing Frasier 2.0, the former NBC sitcom was welcomed back on Paramount+, a lesser-known streaming platform in comparison to Netflix or Peacock. At least it wasn’t Helen Hunt and Paul Reiser’s Mad About You, another ’90s NBC comedy that got its grand return on…Spectrum (?!) in 2019. Girls will air on HBO’s streaming partner, Max, and Glee is in the works via Disney+ and Hulu—barring any major industry mergers.

The Roseanne reboot earned new resonance in the zeitgeist—and major ratings on ABC—for its authentic depiction of a working-class Middle America family under Trump’s first presidency. Like the original 1988 series, the revival focused on the economic and social realities of surviving as a lower-income family in America. And like Will & Grace before it, Roseanne organically, even comically, depicted familial political divides by portraying Roseanne Conner as a Trump voter and her sister Jackie as a Hillary Clinton supporter.

After series lead Roseanne Barr tweeted a racist slur about Valerie Jarrett, a senior aide to President Barack Obama, ABC Entertainment president Channing Dungey terminated the series on May 29, 2018, following its renewal for an 11th season on the network. Then, the following month, ABC announced it was ordering 10 episodes of a spin-off about the family titled The Conners, which regenerated by killing off the character of Roseanne, ending just last year after seven seasons on the air. If anything, the show’s unlikely staying power proves that if a show sticks to its DNA, it can outlast even the messiest of scandals.

The four-episode return of Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel’s mother-daughter dramedy was rightfully docked for its extended, gratuitous Stars Hollow musical involving Tony Award-winning performers (and ex-spouses) Sutton Foster and Christian Borle. But a bit of superfluous song-and-dance naturally feels right at home for Glee, and even Girls—an encore version of Marnie singing Kanye West’s “Stronger” would reach cringeworthy new depths.

The pregnancy revelation that ends Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life should have kicked the revival off, not concluded its story. Instead, A Year in the Life emphasizes just how little Rory and Lorelei have grown in the years since Gilmore Girls ended, only to leave the revival’s most compelling leap forward for its final moments—and totally unresolved. After a decade, the bait-and-switch still burns, which speaks to the divisive, and enduring, nature of TV returns themselves. As for the next chapters of Glee and Girls, may the writers’ rooms hear our post-election pleas.

#3652. Chris Pratt Lost Chuck To Zachary Levi. Years Later, Jurassic World Gave Him A Full-Circle Moment

Being a struggling actor in Hollywood is tough, and even huge stars like Chris Pratt go through the wringer early in their careers (like working at Bubba Gump Shrimp). Such was the case when Pratt lost out on the titular role on the show Chuck. Pratt auditioned for the role in 2007, but lost it to Zachary Levi. That has got to be hard enough, but for Pratt, it was made worse as he was taunted by a billboard for the show in LA. Pratt got the last laugh on the casting directors of the show years later when he got his own poster on the same building for Jurassic World.

After trying out for and not making the final cut for Chuck, things got worse when a billboard Pratt could see from his apartment went up advertising the show, with Levi featured on it. Pratt recently talked about it with Barstool:

I did a screen test for Chuck. I wanted it so bad, and then there was this giant billboard across from my apartment of Zach Levi as Chuck, and I’m like, ‘grrr.’

Imagine waking up every morning and looking out the window at a billboard that you hoped would have your face on it, only to see someone else you lost out to. It would be maddening! Pratt kept at it, of course, and eventually landed gigs in Jennifer’s Body and Moneyball, before really breaking big as part of the ensemble cast of Parks and Rec. It wasn’t until 2015 when the moment came full circle, at the premiere of one of Pratt’s earliest blockbusters, Jurassic World.

The moment wasn’t lost on Pratt, as he explained:

Then that same building is where we had the premiere for Jurassic World. And that same building had a giant poster on it with me on a motorcycle, and I was like, 'whoa!'

That really is coming full circle, from what sounds like a real low point early in his career to the triumph of starring in one of the biggest franchises in Hollywood history. Jurassic World came right on the heels of Pratt joining the MCU as Star-Lord in the first Guardians of the Galaxy, so he had become one of the biggest movie stars on the planet.

So does this mean he’s got a “hidden rivalry” with Levi? Well, probably not. He doesn’t seem to have an animosity towards the Shazam! star, just frustration for not getting a part at that point in his career. It’s safe to say that things have worked out pretty well for Pratt, who will next be seen on the 2026 movie schedule in Way of the Warrior Kid, which will be available to watch with an Apple TV subscription.

#3651. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

Patrick Mahomes and wife Brittany Mahomes’ romance gives Us all the feels — starting with their high school sweetheart beginnings.

The couple started out as two friends in Texas who went to school together. The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback became close with Brittany in 2011 when he was just a freshman at Whitehouse High School.

After dating for several years, the pair attended different colleges but remained an item.
