#3551. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3550. DC Studios' Biggest Superhero Movie Priorities After James Gunn's Exit, Explained

The DC Universe on film is once again under new management, as Warner Bros.' new parent company Skydance has replaced DC Studios co-presidents James Gunn and Peter Safran with Marvel Studios' alum Jeremy Latcham. The reasons for Gunn and Safran's exit are still under scrutiny, but it seems inevitable that whatever plans they had for DC are now going to shift.

According to reporting by The Wrap, Skydance CEO David Ellison is pushing Latcham to focus on DC's A-list characters and get a "Justice League" movie out "as soon as possible." The Wrap adds that even "modestly-known" DC heroes like Supergirl won't be getting the greenlight for now. (The poor box office of "Supergirl" didn't help her specific case.)

One hypothesis for Gunn and Safran's departure, which looks more plausible in light of this reporting, is that they weren't focusing enough on those A-list DC characters. Sure, they started with Superman, but DCU Batman and Wonder Woman movies never moved past development prior to their departure. Making "Clayface," a movie about a B-list Batman villain, before introducing Batman himself is one of those decisions that would be ridiculous to imagine, except it actually happened. It's also a meme among DC fans that Gunn's DCU was frontloading Rick Flag Sr. (Frank Grillo) yet hadn't even introduced the full DC Trinity yet.

But leopards can't change their spots. Gunn's passion for superheroes has always been reinventing C-list characters. Directing for Marvel Studios, he made the Guardians of the Galaxy into household names, and across those movies, it's clear the character he loved most was the biggest oddball among oddballs, Rocket Racoon (Bradley Cooper). He first came to DC directing "The Suicide Squad," and he even packed "Superman" with more obscure DC heroes like Metamorpho (Anthony Carrigan) and Mister Terrific (Edi Gathegi).

In an irony worthy of Alanis Morissette, it appears James Gunn's DCU was finally getting to those A-list characters that David Ellison wants spotlighted. "Lanterns" introduced John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) as Green Lantern, who will be returning in "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow." It's also practically an open secret that Adria Arjona is playing Wonder Woman in "Man of Tomorrow." New reporting suggests that Gunn had also begun writing his third "Superman" movie and was considering tweaking it to a Justice League movie.

Now, I've speculated in the past that if/when Gunn got to the Justice League, he would be basing it on the 1980s comic run "Justice League International" by J.M. DeMatteis, Kevin Maguire and Keith Giffen. That run is basically the blueprint for every James Gunn superhero movie, as it took C-List characters (Booster Gold, Blue Beetle, Guy Gardner Green Lantern, Fire and Ice, etc.) and made their adventures more of a workplace comedy. The JLI was headed up by businessman Maxwell Lord, who appears in "Superman" (played by Sean Gunn) sponsoring the proto Justice League.

But I wouldn't expect that now. DC Studios' "Justice League" movie will surely feature the A-listers: Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, and Aquaman. By largely holding off on those characters, Gunn and Safran may have given Jeremy Latcham more leeway to mold the DCU's headliners.

Now, it's still unclear if DC Studios will do a full continuity reboot or merely a creative pivot. If the latter, it's plausible Corenswet's Superman stays. If Adria Arjona is indeed playing Wonder Woman, a swift recast would probably be awkward, too.

"Lanterns" was also a huge hit for HBO, and TheWrap explicitly names Green Lantern as one of the A-List characters DC Studios is prioritizing. Does that mean Pierre's John Stewart will get a movie?

As for Batman, DC Studios has been in a tight bind with their cash cow the last half-decade. Matt Reeves' "The Batman," commissioned by the previous regime, hit theaters in March 2022, months before James Gunn and Peter Safran's hiring. Gunn was extremely accommodating to Reeves, even as "The Batman Part II" faced numerous scheduling delays. (Reeves has reportedly been dealing with a family crisis, hence him stepping away from shooting "The Batman Part II" as Steven Soderbergh takes over as a stand-in.)

I'm personally grateful we're seeing "The Batman Part II" finished and on Reeves' terms. But the sharper business move would've been to reboot or make Robert Pattinson's Batman part of the DCU. Gunn did neither, only announcing a "Batman" movie, "The Brave and the Bold" in 2023 that never really got rolling. I'd say, now, though, there's a better than likely chance that Reeves and Pattinson's "Batman" series ends with "Part II" to clear the way for a DCU Batman.

So what about the other in-development projects at DC that spotlighted smaller characters, i.e. "Swamp Thing" and the Bane & Deathstroke team-up movie? I think it's a fair bet those are dead. The announced "Teen Titans" movie is a toss-up — the 2003 "Teen Titans" cartoon remains a cultural touchstone for younger millennials and older Gen Zers, but the team might still fit into the "modestly known" box like Supergirl apparently does.

For better or worse, DC fans should expect to see the Justice League back onscreen sooner rather than later.

DC’s Lanterns made quite a splash amid the 2026 TV schedule, as the HBO superhero drama received critical acclaim and strong viewership numbers. Since the show’s eight-episode season wrapped up in early October, fans have been wondering whether a second season might happen. Now, viewers may have even more questions about what’s going on, considering James Gunn is leaving his CEO post at DC Studios. Now, Lanterns showrunner Chris Mundy is weighing in on Gunn’s departure and Lanterns’ future.

As the head of DC Studios, Gunn was one of the driving creative forces behind Lanterns, and both he and co-CEO Peter Safran are credited as executive producers. Mundy, of course, worked with the pair to lay out the direction of the series. Mundy was recently interviewed by The Playlist and was directly asked about Gunn’s exit after the Paramount/Warner Bros. merger and whether it could spell the end of his superhero show. Mundy answered honestly but, sadly, his comments don’t inspire much confidence:

We thought everything had settled [after the merger]. I can imagine a world where everyone retreats to their corners, but then, you know, it's a coin flip, 50/50.

Lanterns’ fate hasn’t been officially confirmed, as of this writing. Yet, based on Mundy’s sentiments, it’s hard not to get the feeling that the writing may be on the wall. As someone who enjoyed the show – which also counts Damon Lindelof and Tom King as EPs – I was eager to see another set of episodes. Prior to the Gunn news breaking, it had already been reported that a writers’ room was being assembled for Season 2, but Safran also said the season would only happen if there was a story worthy of being told.

Upcoming DC TV Shows: Full List Of Series In 2026 And Beyond, Including The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd

Mundy and co.’s show predominantly centers on John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), a young man hoping to join the Green Lantern Corps. At the same time, Stewart receives “training” from prickly veteran Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler), who fears being replaced by the young man. Ahead of the show’s debut, Gunn and the creative team described it as a grounded adventure in the vein of True Detective. Some fans were displeased, however, not just with the lack of green in early footage but with the eventual revelation of Jordan’s death (which Gunn defended).

It was always intended for John Stewart to become a big part of the DCU moving forward, as the newly minted Green Lantern is returning in Man of Tomorrow, which will be released in 2027. Beyond that, however, plans for the continuity as a whole remain uncertain due to Gunn and Safran being ushered out and Jeremy Latcham entering as CEO by Dec. 1. Based on some of the fan reactions to Gunn’s exit, they’re not confident Lanterns will be back for another season.

Needless to say, I’m not sure Chris Mundy’s remarks will necessarily make fans feel hopeful about the future of the show. Of course, the Green Lantern-centric series is just one piece of a larger puzzle regarding the future of DC Studios. I’ll be eager to see what Latcham and the head honchos at Skydance have to say about their plans and whether they include Pierre’s version of Stewart.

Lanterns is now available to stream in its entirety with an HBO Max subscription. Fans can also head over to that streamer to check out more DC shows, those connected to the DCU and those that are not.

#3548. Who Is Jeremy Latcham? Everything We Know About The New Head Of DC Studios

As Hollywood reels from the shock of James Gunn and Peter Safran getting shown the door at DC Studios, the industry is trying to get a bead on how their replacement, Jeremy Latcham, will approach the job. It's highly unlikely he'll continue with Gunn and Safran's development slate, though if Gunn's "Superman" sequel, "Man of Tomorrow," does significantly better than the first film at the box office, there could be a possibility he'll let Gunn close out a potential trilogy. Latcham is also inheriting HBO shows like "Lanterns" and "The People v. Gorilla Grodd," and as of this writing, neither has been greenlit for a second season.

Like most executives do when they take over a studio, Latcham is reportedly poised to wipe the slate clean and put his personal stamp on whatever comes next. Latcham is no stranger to making superhero movies. He was one of Kevin Feige's right-hand men at Marvel Studios, where he helped his boss set the "Avengers Initiative" in motion with "Iron Man." His track record is strong, and he's well regarded as a no-bulls*** guy. If Skydance executive David Ellison and his production executives Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg were going to take a chance on someone who'd never run a Hollywood studio before, Latcham at least had a promising pedigree.

As for that personal stamp, it's fair to wonder if Latcham's strong Christian faith will impact the types of filmmakers he pursues to, presumably, make his all-new iterations of Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman. Talking with the Bible Bros about his work for the faith-based Wonder Project, where he helped develop "Flyer" (an uplifting biopic about the Wright Brothers) and the Biblical TV series "House of David," Latcham expressed a desire to make movies that meant something to him. How will this gibe with mainstream moviegoers, many of whom aren't Christian?

During that BibleBros appearance, Latcham said, "Let's be the HBO for the faith and family audience. Let's try to make movies and television shows that restore faith in things worth believing in." As we've seen over the last couple of decades, there's definitely an audience for this. But a successful faith-based company like Angel Studios has never made a movie that's sniffed $1 billion worldwide. Not even close.

At Marvel, Latcham was famous for asking if his grandmother would approve of certain moments or the overall themes of MCU movies. As he told the Bible Bros, "That became the stand-in for, like, 'Is this going to work for regular people that are outside the bubble of Hollywood? Is this safe for a regular family?" He went on to say that his grandmother's pastor gave a sermon on how "Iron Man" was an effective tale of redemption.

Right now, the clearest indication we have of how Latcham will run DC Studios comes from his Bible Bros visit, where he extolled virtues of "faith in God, obviously, faith in country, faith in family, faith in fathers, faith in all these institutions that we believe in in America. The idea of America, the idea of a democratic, free capitalist society." He then added that he'd like to make these virtues "front and center" in his movies.

Latcham has strong ties with many notable filmmakers and actors who seem to genuinely like him. He certainly comes off as very likable in his interviews. But he's got one heck of a challenge ahead of him. DC Studios is rebooting for the third time in 13 years, and moviegoers certainly have a case of superhero fatigue. They'll show up for Batman and Spider-Man and events like an "Avengers" installment, but if you keep pulling the rug out from under your audience, they will eventually abandon you.

Matt Reeves' "The Batman: Part II" is guaranteed to be a massive hit when it arrives in 2028, but the first film probably didn't go down well with Latcham's grandmother. I have no idea what a Latcham Batman will look like, but that hardcore fan base expects the Caped Crusader to go hard. Take your foot off the gas, and you might see grosses on par with "Batman & Robin."

Latcham has the added burden of reporting to Greenstein and Goldberg, who report to CEO David Ellison, who seemingly wants broad-appeal blockbusters with as little artistry as possible. Latcham knows how this works from his Marvel Studios days, but he was just one voice in their by-committee process. He'll assemble his own team, and we'll just have to wait and see what that looks like. In the meantime, it'll be interesting to see what kind of directors and stars he pursues, as well as which properties he prioritizes. He'd do well to look at Gunn's "Superman" and go for a tone that's tough but fun and hopeful. And while he has every right to imbue these movies with elements of his faith, he needs to be careful not to alienate people who don't worship at his church. Because that's a small bubble, too.

#3547. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3546. Exclusive: ‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte, in His Own Words

For those of us who managed to land a role on Breaking Bad, the show is a formative part of our lives. It represented a chance to work on what is now considered one of the best shows TV has ever seen, and the cast and crew forged an unbreakable bond. RJ Mitte was part of the show’s heartbeat. When I spoke to him for this book, we reflected on our days shooting in New Mexico fondly.

I’ll always remember him as a young kid—bright, talented, and a real sweetheart—who was so thrilled to be on set with us that it reminded us how lucky we all were. We'll all miss him dearly. Rest in peace, RJ. —Dean Norris

The last person to join the White family was RJ Mitte, cast in the role of Walt Jr., aka “Flynn.” RJ, who was only fourteen years old at the time, joined the project after we had already begun filming the pilot, following multiple rounds of auditions stretching out over several months. You might wonder why casting Walt Jr., a comparatively minor character among the core cast, took so long. Well, it was about verisimilitude. As written, Walt Jr. had cerebral palsy, albeit a relatively minor case. It was a fundamental part of the character, and Vince was adamant that the role not be played by a nondisabled actor.

VINCE GILLIGAN, creator: I was worried at the beginning that people wouldn’t connect with Walt. They’d say, Why is this guy doing this terrible thing? And so I kind of loaded him up for bear in terms of, you know, he had a son with cerebral palsy. You felt bad for him. People bullied him.

SHARON BIALY, casting director: We had a lot of autonomy with casting, once we knew what Vince was looking for, once we all agreed that, aesthetically, we were talking about the same type of actor. A case in point is RJ Mitte’s role. Vince only wanted actors who had CP. So, we conducted a nationwide search.

RJ MITTE, Walt Jr.: Walt Jr. is actually based on a real person, a friend of Vince’s from college who had cerebral palsy. So, Vince was really particular about the role of Walt Jr. and who was going to play him.

Experienced actors who also have mild CP is not the deepest pool, of course, but there are more candidates than you might expect. And RJ Mitte’s casting has to be considered something of a surprise, given his relative lack of experience and a variety of other challenges he faced while growing up.

RJ MITTE: We were living in Houston when my sister got discovered at a water park, and that’s what brought us to LA. My sister got booked on a job at Universal Studios for an ad campaign. She was one and a half at the time. We really didn’t have a lot going on. Things were tough. My mom was a single mom, and she had recently been partially paralyzed in a car accident, and my grandparents, who I was very close to, were both sick and dying, so when we got this offer to go to LA, we took it. It was a paid trip. They put us up in a motel in Hollywood—there was a strip club on one side, and a Ralphs and a library on the other side. That’s LA.

Everything was covered for six months, so I just started acting to meet kids my own age and have a little extra cash while we were there. And it ended up turning into a career for me. I started working at a young age, not in the acting industry, but with my uncle and family jobs and stuff to make money as a young kid. I would like to think I grew up with a strong work ethic. So, when we got to LA, I hit the ground running. Within the first six months, I was on shows like Hannah Montana, Everybody Hates Chris, Weeds, Seventh Heaven, Drillbit Taylor, Epic Movie—­ all as an extra. I think that really helped prepare me for Breaking Bad, just with the quality of work and the type of professionalism that the set had. I’m very grateful, because if I did not get Breaking Bad, I wouldn’t have an acting career.

At any number of points along the journey, RJ’s dream could have died. It’s hard enough for a known actor to land a role in a show of this quality, but for a newcomer, it must have been daunting, although you never would have known it by the way he carried himself on set.

RJ MITTE: Funny story: My very first audition ever in my career was an anti­ meth campaign for the state of California. It was a wild PSA, and I ended up not getting it. A year or so later, I started auditioning for Breaking Bad. The description of the role literally said, “dark hair, big eyebrows, and mild cerebral palsy.” And I was like, that’s me!

Sharon Bialy called me in, and I already had been on quite a few auditions by that point, and I didn’t book any of them, so I knew what rejection felt like. I had a sense of, Don’t hold your breath. But I’m a firm believer that you go in owning it and when you walk out, don’t look back. Every callback was a little more like, Wait, I’m actually still in the running.

Walt Jr. had a somewhat more severe case of CP than RJ, who did not use assistive devices for mobility in real life.

RJ MITTE: When I went in for my first audition, Sharon was there, and she had hurt her foot. So, she actually handed me her crutches that she was using for the audition. Six months went by, four callbacks, four auditions, and in that final one, they’re like, Okay, we’re sending you. You’re going to New Mexico. The next day I was on a 6 a.m. flight to audition for Vince and the team. Then he excused me for a moment and brought me back in to do my test screening with Anna and Bryan.

Think about that. RJ was fourteen years old and trying to land a job that would change his life, a job that would help him support his entire family. Talk about pressure.

RJ MITTE: I think in life I’ve always had pressure. It really didn’t stand out to me too much. I can only do what I can do. And so as long as I’m doing my best, that’s what matters. But it always kind of felt like I was part of the team to some degree, even when I wasn’t. And so when it came to doing the scene with Anna and Bryan, it really felt like a family. It was like, Oh, yeah, this feels right. Apparently, they must have had the same feeling because they hired me.

Like everyone else, RJ made the most of his opportunity and crafted a fully formed portrait of an adolescent at the center of a family storm; one whose disability may have helped shape him but did not define who he was.

RJ MITTE: This was the first time I think people really saw a character with a disability who wasn’t disabled. There’s nothing he couldn’t do that other kids were doing. It wasn’t about the disability, and that’s something that I think Vince really stressed: it’s not about his disability; it’s about being a part of the family and living with it.

Five seasons in, Breaking Bad reached its apotheosis with the monumental episode “Ozymandias,” in which Walter White’s house of cards comes crashing down. It’s also the episode where Flynn learns the truth about his father’s double life, and that Walt has led my character—his brother-in-law, Hank—to his death. The episode builds to a climactic moment where Flynn’s mother, Skyler, grabs a knife and brandishes it at her husband.

RIAN JOHNSON, director, “Ozymandias”: The actual fight itself, I remember being surprisingly fun to shoot—­just making sure to give Anna and Bryan the space that they needed to find it. I think RJ also did a terrific job in that moment—­ he’s kind of the linchpin of the whole thing.

It is indeed Flynn who rises to the occasion. When Walt wrestles the knife away from Skyler, his son jumps on top of him and throws him across the room. He’s a big kid, strong enough to handle Walt despite his disability; strong enough to protect his mother.

RJ MITTE: It was very intense to shoot. At the same time, we’re professionals. Everything was very choreographed. There was one moment when we first started, I got so heated, and so into it, that I kind of accidentally grabbed Bryan the wrong way and kind of like tossed him . . . wrong. And everyone was like, “Whoa, RJ! You can’t throw him like that.” And I was like, “Oh, I’m so sorry. I just got caught up in the moment.”

RIAN JOHNSON: When you see Walt Jr. turn, then you know it’s truly over. And Bryan’s reaction to that just breaks my heart every time I see it.

In the series’s penultimate episode, Walt clandestinely calls Flynn at school. A package is on its way, he says, to be delivered to the home of one of Flynn’s friends. The package contains money, one hundred thousand dollars—­the most he could stuff into one box. “I wanted to give you so much more, but this is all I could do,” Walt explains, leaning into the pay phone as Flynn listens, wordlessly, on the other end.

RJ MITTE: I remember at the time we were shooting that scene it was in this school-slash-doctor’s-office that we were using. Bryan was in the room with me when we did this part. It definitely was heartbreaking to have to feel that way about someone that I admire. And I think that’s what Junior felt as well. I’m a believer that in life, there’s always a moment where you have to choose to either be an adult or to stay a child. This moment comes in many different forms, but it comes down to that moment where you say, Am I going to accept this and give them what they want and be submissive, and still have that child aspect of who I am? Or am I going to take charge and become the person that I need to be—­ the man, the adult?

RJ does some terrific wordless acting in this scene, wrestling with this decision. Then he speaks: “Just shut up! Just stop it. Stop it. I don’t want anything from you.”

“You need this money,” Walt says. “Your mother needs this money. It can’t all be for nothing.”

Yes, it can, as Flynn makes abundantly clear.

RJ MITTE: A lot of the decisions I made for Junior were based on my own experiences as a young adult. At the time I was still a child, but I utilized those moments from my own life of having to stand my ground and make that decision—­ realizing who I am and what I need to do to take care and provide for my family. In the show, Walt was no longer doing that. He was actually creating more danger for his family.

I think it’s very powerful that Walt Jr. had the ability to stand his ground, and to put those boundaries in place: “You’re out. This is my family now, and you’re not a part of it.” I find a lot of young men and women have to take that stance at some point, especially with parents or family figures that live in a volatile world, a world that is corrupt.

Later, in the series finale, Walt is standing over a crib, caressing the hair of baby Holly as she naps. He leaves and then watches from a distance as Flynn gets off a school bus and walks into the apartment.

VINCE GILLIGAN: With Walt, you want him to have a goodbye scene with his wife. We were sad we couldn’t have a goodbye scene with his son, Walt Jr., because RJ is a wonderful actor. We just didn’t have the room.

For those of us who were fortunate enough to be a part of it, Breaking Bad remains a seminal event in our lives, both personally and professionally—­ an opportunity to work on one of the greatest television shows in history, alongside people who became lifelong friends.

BRYAN CRANSTON: I knew when it ended that this was the role of my life.

AARON PAUL: I think I can speak for everyone involved in the show: It changed all of our lives.

RJ MITTE: I will be eighty years old in a nursing home and there will probably be someone looking at me through a window, saying, “There’s Walt Jr.” And I’m okay with that.

Excerpted from the book DO WHAT YOU’RE GONNA DO: The Definitive Oral History of Breaking Bad by Dean Norris with Joe Layden. Copyright © 2026 by Dean Norris. From William Morrow, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Reprinted by permission.

It's an exciting time in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Fresh off VisionQuest's run for those with a Disney+ subscription, folks are looking forward to the upcoming Marvel movie release of Avengers: Doomsday. Folks are excited to see entire teams of heroes make up the Doomsday cast, although Kevin Feige confirmed more surprise characters are coming. In a recent interview Anthony Mackie might have spoiled one of those secret appearances.

What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is limited, so there are countless fans and theories about what The Russo Brothers might have up their sleeve. In a clip from ET's Twitter, Mackie spoke about the experience of shooting the mysterious blockbuster offering:

These movies, they're like summer camp. You know, everybody comes together. And it's 'Oh how have you been? Oh, you have a kid now. Oh you're married now.' It's one of those things where you catch up with everybody. I got to hang out with Paul Bettany, who I love.

You hung out with WHO?! Hardcore Marvel fans will know that there's been no official confirmation of Paul Bettany appearing in Avengers: Doomsday. So if Mackie didn't misspeak here, this is huge news that Vision could seemingly appear in the highly anticipated crossover event. Coming straight off VisionQuest, this is a thrilling concept that's sure to quickly go viral.

Only time will tell if the studio responds to these comments, or if we'll have to wait until December to see if Bettany actually appears in the next Avengers flick. The actor has had a very long history with the MCU, starting by voicing J.A.R.V.I.S. in the first Iron Man movie. So it would be thrilling to see him join the battle against Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom.

Tom Holland is known for accidentally revealing Marvel spoilers, but he might have some competition if Paul Bettany ends up showing up in Doomsday. If Mackie did spill the beans, he'd be in good company, as Mark Ruffalo went so far as to accidentally spoil Infinity War's twist ending.

Marvel is known for its tight security, and the contents of The Russo Brothers' movie is being especially kept under wraps. Although as we get closer to its December release, more information is sure to start trickling out. Only time will tell how many surprise characters end up appearing that weren't in the cast list. I mean just look at Chris Evans' Steve Rogers, who got his own trailer after it leaked online.

Our answers will come when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. If Mackie's comments are to be believed, we should expect to see Paul Bettany appear. But considering how many characters he's portrayed in the shared universe, there's no guarantee he'll actually be Vision. My head is truly spinning from all the possibilities.

#3544. The Big Bang Theory's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

Ever since it ended in 2019, "The Big Bang Theory," the CBS sitcom created by Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady, has remained exceedingly popular. Not only is it still a hit on its exclusive streaming home (HBO Max), it's spawned two prequel spin-offs ("Young Sheldon" and "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage"), creating a small-screen cinematic universe. So did it ever jump the shark? Yeah, and I'll tell you how, when, and why.

At the beginning of "The Big Bang Theory," Sheldon Cooper and Leonard Hofstadter (Jim Parsons and Johnny Galecki) meet their new neighbor Penny (Kaley Cuoco), with whom Leonard is immediately smitten. Despite a rocky start, Penny and Sheldon ultimately overcome their differences and become good friends. More than that, Penny is a sort of audience surrogate, helping translate Sheldon and Leonard's nerdiness — as well as that of their friends Howard Wolowitz (Simon Helberg) and Raj Koothrappali (Kunal Nayyar) — for the masses. The guys work together at the California Institute of Technology as physicists, engineers, and astrophysicists, and spend their time reading comic books.

Eventually, Melissa Rauch and Mayim Bialik join the series as microbiologist Bernadette Rostenkowski and neuroscientist Amy Farrah Fowler, and they add some much-needed feminine energy to the proceedings — and give Penny some much-needed storylines that don't center around the guys. (Helberg agrees that they generally improved the series too.) Unfortunately, though, Amy and Bernadette's introduction on "The Big Bang Theory" was the beginning of the end for the show's better years. The downfall of "The Big Bang Theory" doesn't quite kick off at the end of Season 5 when Howard and Bernadette tie the knot, but when others start following suit, the quality decline is obvious. The real downfall, though, is the Season 9 premiere.

At the beginning of "The Big Bang Theory" Season 9, Leonard and Penny hastily decide to get married at a Las Vegas wedding chapel — without any of their friends or family present. The whole thing is weird, and honestly, the Season 9 premiere "The Matrimonial Momentum" is one of the show's all-time worst episodes). On the drive there, Leonard admits that he kissed another woman during a lengthy research trip in the North Sea two years beforehand, and Penny is understandably upset to discover that her then-boyfriend cheated on her and hid it from her for years. Still, they determinedly go through with the chapel wedding anyway, culminating in a less-than-satisfying wedding night at a Vegas hotel and the two returning to their respective apartments to sleep separately when they get back to Pasadena.

So, this episode stinks, but it also points to a much bigger structural problem in later seasons of "The Big Bang Theory." Once everyone starts pairing off, the show focuses less on the genuinely delightful interplay between the entire cast, and we get way more storylines about relationship problems, which start to feel flat-out repetitive and boring. By the time Penny and Leonard have their second wedding (with their loved ones in attendance) in the Season 10 premiere and Amy and Sheldon get married in the Season 11 finale, "The Big Bang Theory" is stuck in a cycle, especially because Howard and Bernadette have children in that same timeframe. As "The Big Bang Theory" pairs off all of its main characters (except poor Raj), it experiences a fall from greatness and becomes a run-of-the-mill sitcom ... and also makes one issue glaringly obvious.

There is not, and I'm not exaggerating, one healthy couple to be found within the later seasons of "The Big Bang Theory." Even after Leonard and Penny finally get together and stay that way, they have to get married twice after that botched first attempt. They constantly disagree on major issues like having children and career choices, and Leonard still sees himself as intellectually superior to Penny. Howard does put his time as a wannabe womanizer behind him and settle down with Bernadette, but throughout their marriage he proves to be a total manchild who was coddled by his mother for so long that he expects the same treatment from Bernadette. Then there's Sheldon and Amy, who experience the slowest-moving relationship possible due to Sheldon's issues with physical intimacy. This is a very real thing that could have been explored with sensitivity, but instead, Sheldon treats Amy like a sick, depraved pervert for wanting to sleep with her romantic partner — and the show does the same by extension, making her desire for more physicality with Sheldon into a running joke.

"The Big Bang Theory" features a ton of terrible relationship behavior. It almost exclusively comes from the male partners, and it almost all occurs from Season 9 onwards. That's why the downfall of "The Big Bang Theory" can be pinned to that terrible Season 9 premiere, which isn't just an uncomfortable, awkward, and largely unfunny half hour of the series — it's a stark indicator of the doldrums that follow as the show reaches its endpoint.

"The Big Bang Theory" is streaming on HBO Max now.

#3543. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Is Already the Second-Best-Selling Switch 2 Game

The remake sold 5.2 million copies in 4 days, eclipsing Donkey Kong Bananza

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the fastest-selling Switch 2 game yet. On Wednesday, Nintendo announced that the remake of the 1998 classic sold more than 5.2 million copies worldwide in its first four days on sale — "the highest global sales for any Nintendo-published Nintendo Switch 2 game in its first four days."

This also means that Ocarina of Time is likely already the second-best-selling Switch 2 game, period. Mario Kart World has sold over 16 million copies, but according to Nintendo's most recent financial figures, its second-best-selling title through the end of September was Donkey Kong Bananza, with 5.05 million copies sold.

Nintendo only publishes sales figures for its own titles; it's possible that a third-party game has sold more than Ocarina and Bananza, although it's hard to imagine what that might be.

Ocarina of Time is only Nintendo's second-biggest hit of 2026 so far, though. Tomodachi Life, for the original Switch, remains the champ for now with an amazing 8.8 million copies sold. Even so, Ocarina will likely eclipse it before the end of the year.

After a somewhat controversial reveal, due to its radically different art style, Ocarina of Time has been met with widespread critical acclaim and looks like a strong awards contender, too.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

60 Minutes has entered a new era amid the 2026 TV schedule, and a person who’s been overseeing much of the work behind the scenes is CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss. In conjunction with the news magazine show’s EP, Nick Bilton, Weiss has been looking to update the program, and those efforts have been accompanied by major staff changes and backlash. Some of the criticisms have come from former staff members, including ex-EP Bill Owens, who recently shared his biggest concerns over the series he once shepherded.

Owens worked at CBS News for 37 years and, in 2019, he was named the EP of 60 Minutes after having spent 12 years overseeing its content in other roles. He ultimately resigned from his post in April 2025 amid a flurry of behind-the-scenes changes at 60. Since his departure, Owens has discussed his time with the show, and he notably shared thoughts ahead of the Season 59 premiere, which aired in September. At Semafor’s New Media & Marketing Playbook event, Owens was asked for his thoughts on his former workplace and said:

Not a lot. [Skydance owns] the company, they can do whatever they want. But the ratings are telling. There’s no doubt that linear television is in decline. But the numbers the other day were less than 6 million people. It’s like the evening news. 60 Minutes? That would have freaked me out.

Ratings for the latest season of 60 have reportedly been down compared to those of Season 58. The season premiere notched lower viewership and, despite some forward progress in subsequent weeks, more recent numbers haven’t been so strong. For instance, per data on the show’s October 25 broadcast, the episode only drew 5.6 million live viewers, which fell well below Season 58’s 9.1 million average. Despite that, when Bari Weiss addressed concerns, she stated that the show was doing “tremendously well.”

As for Owens, he’s been candid about leaving 60 Minutes, and he has attributed that move to no longer having the editorial independence he and his colleagues had long been granted. During the Semafor event, Owens also criticized the show’s interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and argued that better questions should’ve been asked. On a separate note, the veteran journalist also admitted that he wished his departure would’ve had a different effect on 60:

When I left, I really hoped that I was going to cause enough of a commotion that they would kind of back off. And the people, my senior team, the correspondents, they’ve tried their best. But it’s just a really difficult circumstance.

May 2026 marked the beginning of major personnel changes at 60 Minutes, as several high-profile staffers were let go, including correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega as well as former EP Tanya Simon. Days later, fellow host Scott Pelley was fired as well after he reportedly accused Weiss of “murdering” the show. Around that time, Owens defended Pelley’s comments, saying that he “stood up the way that I did a year ago and I couldn’t be prouder of him, and I know all the people at 60 Minutes couldn’t be prouder of him.”

Bill Owens has since moved on to other ventures and, beginning in March 2027, he’ll executive-produce a YouTube-based outlet known as NewPress. It’s also been rumored that Owens will spill tea about his time at 60 Minutes through a tell-all memoir, but that’s yet to materialize. At the very least, though, Owens still seems somewhat interested about what the future holds for 60.

#3540. Sonia Gandhi Gives an Intimate Account of Her Husband Rajiv Gandhi’s Final Days and Assassination

A week later the general elections were announced for May 1991. Rajiv was soon immersed in work on the party manifesto and meetings to decide on the Congress candidates. He was well aware of the grave danger he was exposed to from diverse terrorist groups. But it was his task to lead his forces in the electoral battle. As he said whenever the subject came up of the threat to his life, “If it comes to having to die for what one believes in, I don’t hesitate.”

As president of the Congress Party, he would have to cover thirty thousand kilometers and more than six hundred parliamentary and assembly constituencies, in every region and almost every state of the country. It was going to be the longest stretch of time we’d be apart from each other in all the years of our marriage. With him being on the move constantly, in those pre-smartphone days I’d get news from his staff and only occasionally hear directly from him.

If I was exhausted from the one campaign, he was that much more so from weeks of being on the go for almost twenty hours a day. He hadn’t been able to eat or sleep properly, as often one day’s program slipped without break into the next. Rather than cancel an engagement, he’d snatch some rest by closing his eyes briefly in between. On some days he used a small plane or helicopter to cover the distances, occasionally piloting the aircraft. On other days he drove long distances by car, addressing scores of formal and informal meetings, at times till the small hours of the day.

Everywhere he was mobbed and his schedule frequently delayed. I felt stricken to see his hands and arms badly scratched and swollen, his body bruised and aching from all the hugs and handshakes he had received from well-wishers. Stretched out with a bolster under his feet, he talked to us about his punishing tours, and how much he was looking forward to the closing of the campaign. When I asked him, “Do you think we have a good chance?” he answered tentatively, “It’s going to be a tough fight, let’s see . . .” Our daughter, Priyanka, and I were glad to tell him that we were confident of a victory for him in his constituency.

On the morning of May 20, we drove together to the polling booth to cast our vote. On the way back I told him how flustered I’d been looking for the spot where I had to place my mark. The ballot paper was a large sheet, and I was confused by the plethora of party symbols printed on it. For a moment I even thought I’d have to forgo giving him my vote. He laughed, holding my hand with that gentle touch that never failed to dispel my anxiety.

He left for another day’s tour and was scheduled to touch down at Delhi airport later, just to change from a helicopter to a plane that would take him to Orissa. I was excited to get a sudden message that he’d come home briefly at around four fifteen in the afternoon. He had a quick bath and a snack; then it was time to leave. He spoke on the phone to our son, Rahul, to wish him well for a coming test and cautioned him lovingly to be careful about his safety. He said goodbye to Priyanka, then suddenly turned to me, and said, “Why don’t you come with me?” I was tempted for a moment, then replied, “I’m still very tired, Rajiv. I’ll see you when you get back.” “All right,” he laughed. “It’s just two more days anyway.” He was scheduled to return for a break before going on to the last stage of campaigning.

This picture of us embracing in a tree was by a friend.

We gave each other a goodbye hug and he left. I watched him, as was my habit, from behind the curtain, till he disappeared from view. It’s more than thirty years since that fateful evening. I still find it searing to revisit those events. Some parts remain a blur in my mind. I thought then and afterwards, many times—why, why didn’t I go with him? My last living image of him is his smile as he looks back, waves to me, and steps into the car that will drive him to the airport.

Rajiv had completed his campaign rallies in Bhubaneshwar in Orissa, flown to Andhra Pradesh for more rallies, and then was going to Madras (renamed Chennai five years later). He was informed that the plane that was to fly him to Tamil Nadu had developed a snag, then came a second message that it was now in order. He reached Madras and immediately set off by road towards a small town then unknown to most people called Sriperumbudur. That was going to be his last engagement of the day. He’d already covered many important places in the state, but he didn’t want to disappoint the candidate, a senior Congress Party representative, Maragatham Chandrashekhar; she had pleaded with him to stop there for just a brief meeting.

He stepped out of the car to meet party workers who had lined up to welcome him. He walked down the receiving line and was asked by one of the workers to pause and listen to her daughter recite him a poem. Smiling, he cheerfully agreed. Next in line was a woman holding a garland who motioned as if to offer it to him. As he bent his head to receive it, she detonated the explosives strapped to her body. The explosion killed him and fourteen others in his vicinity, as well as the assassin, and injured another forty-three. It was May 20, 1991, and Rajiv was forty-six years old; three months later we would have celebrated his forty-seventh birthday.

My recollection of many details of that time is sketchy. I was so overwhelmed by panic and pain that for years they absented themselves from my memory. As hard as I tried, it was like attempting to read words on a blank piece of paper. Much later, some moments returned to my mind, but to this day my own memories here are mixed with what has been recounted to me by my daughter and others. Some images are etched clearly in my mind, others are blurred and disjointed. I remember that at some point during that night of horror I dragged myself through the corridor towards the porch and drew aside the curtain on the main door to look for Priyanka. I saw a cluster of staff members huddled together, sobbing, tears streaming down their faces, the children’s nanny, Ongmu, wailing loudly. I retreated; my head was spinning. I could barely feel my legs. I was about to fall. Priyanka saw me; she held me up and took me to her room, made me sit on her bed.

On May 27 Rahul, Priyanka, and I set out with relatives and friends by a special train for Allahabad. We travel through the night, an exhausting journey broken by frequent stops. At every break crowds of mourners surge forward for a glimpse of the urn containing Rajiv’s ashes. We reach his constituency, Amethi, at three thirty in the morning. People are waiting, grieving and disconsolate. They had placed their trust in him, shared their pains, hopes, and aspirations with him. They had given him their vote and wanted to see him return as their prime minister. Instead, they are paying their last tearful tribute to their leader’s ashes.

We reach Allahabad later on the morning of May 28 and are driven to Rajiv’s ancestral home. We place the urn on the platform where the ashes of his grandfather, his brother, and his mother had been placed before. In the afternoon we are taken by boat to the sacred Sangam for the immersion.

Two decades earlier, on a pearly dawn, we had set off—Rajiv, his brother Sanjay, and I—on a boat ride to the Sangam at my mother-in-law’s request. Rajiv had pointed out the different colors of the water, the mood of the two rivers, one almost resisting merging with the other. He had explained the religious belief in a third river, the invisible Saraswati flowing below the mighty Ganga and the Yamuna. Finally he had guided me through the meaning of the ritual that we were then to perform.

On this day we are taken on a boat towards the Sangam—Rahul, Priyanka, and I. Crowds on other boats encircle us, chanting Rajiv’s name. We reach a platform raised over the water. We clamber onto it with others, amidst Vedic chanting. Rahul, with the priest by his side, empties his father’s ashes into the river. Priyanka holds me tenderly as my tears blind me to the scene. A military band plays “Abide with Me,” one of Mahatma Gandhi’s favorite hymns. We are taken to the shore and then back to Swaraj Bhawan.

I find Rajiv’s travel bag—someone had brought it back. He had always packed his own bags, whether for official or personal tours—as his mother had brought him up to do things on his own. My heart racing, I open it: two khadi kurta sets, handkerchiefs, a shawl, his underclothes neatly folded. His little toilet bag, toothbrush and shaver, his hairbrush, dark glasses, and a portable radio. In an inside zippered compartment, the portable array of family photographs he always carried with him—the first picture he took of me in Cambridge, and later ones. I look at them one by one: the children at different stages of their growing up, his mother and brother. A separate bag has the clothes he had changed out of. I bend over it, seeking to inhale the elusive scent of my beloved, gone forever.

Rahul and Priyanka supporting me at Rajiv’s funeral in 1991

Many of Rajiv’s friends had also come to attend his funeral. I met them briefly with the children. We were touched that some of them had come all the way from distant countries to bid him their last farewell. They were friends from his time in Cambridge as well as from his school days and his years as a pilot. It was a testament to the bond that had kept them close through the years.

My maternal uncles, my mother, and my sister Nadia had come, too, and both my sisters’ estranged husbands. Mother and Nadia stayed back after the funeral to comfort and support us. From the time they first met Rajiv, they had loved him and looked to him as the special human being he was—caring, joyful, always ready to cheer up and help others, his beautiful eyes and smile a reflection of his inner being.

At times over the next few weeks I could feel a certain restlessness in Nadia. A few days before her departure, while sitting in the drawing room in the afternoon, the two of us alone, she began to talk about our young days when I was still at home before I went to Cambridge—how she always looked up to me and admired me, even though she’d tell tales to our mother on her older sisters, of our games, of my helping her with her homework, of Rajiv when she first saw him.

Suddenly she became very serious and, looking straight into my eyes, she exclaimed, “Sonia, they killed your mother-in-law, now they have killed your husband. What are you still doing here? What are you waiting for? For your children’s turn, and yours? India has brought you so much sorrow. Come home, Sonia, we all want you to come back [to Italy].”

I was stunned by her words. For a moment I couldn’t even speak, but as I regained my composure, I replied firmly, “No, Nadia, no! You can’t understand. This is my home. It is my country, my children’s country.”

#3538. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Review: Prime Video's Lord Of The Rings Series Still Falls Short

If there's one theme the latest installment of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" highlights above the rest, it's this: Time comes for us all. Whether it's the glacial pace experienced by immortal Elves or the nonstop blur the rest of Middle-earth's mere mortals have been doomed (or gifted?) to receive, this army's inevitable march is one that nobody — not even a Dark Lord — can hope to defeat.

Four years after the Prime Video series first made waves among a passionate, if divisive fanbase, it's clear co-showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have felt this pressure as keenly as anyone. An up-and-down debut season with glimpses of potential eventually found itself surpassed by a sophomore effort that went darker, bolder, and better than before. But, to date, fans have been left waiting for the moment when this J.R.R. Tolkien adaptation truly comes into its own.

Time, unfortunately, is a commodity that "The Rings of Power" doesn't have on its side this year. There's Amazon's head-scratching release strategy that (mostly) becomes clear in retrospect, with eight episodes of streaming television squeezed into three total weeks. More troublingly, the actual story does itself very few favors. There are simply too many far-flung locations to check in on, too many main characters and uninteresting supporting players to service, too much nerdy lore for casuals to digest (if any are even left) ... and, despite some of the most sluggish pacing in streaming, there's hardly enough space to let them breathe. It's an issue that rears its ugly, Balrog-shaped head again and again.

In short, Season 3 is an encapsulation of "The Rings of Power" as a whole: some incredibly high highs, several frustrating lows, and the creeping feeling that time is finally starting to run out.

Season 3's big claim to fame has been heavily teased as the creation of the legendary One Ring, which is the one doomsday event overshadowing over every single storyline this year. Five years after the conclusion of Season 2, as Galadriel's exposition-dump narration explains in the premiere, Sauron's armies wage war on the rest of Middle-earth. Only the Elves and their magical, untarnished rings remain capable of holding out. But when a suspicious Orc arrives (Adam Young as Marnûkh, easily one of the season's best new additions) bearing game-changing news of Sauron's plans, this kicks off a series of events that will either lead to good's greatest triumph over evil ... or as stunning a failure as anything in Tolkien's legendarium.

As a prequel, of course, "The Rings of Power" uses our knowledge of what's to come in "The Lord of the Rings" to its advantage. As a result, every moment Sauron is on screen trying (and failing) to forge his superweapon to rule them all absolutely soars. Whether he's cruelly bossing powerless underlings around, casually committing murder, arguing with the ghosts in his head, or generally sulking over his inability to seduce Galadriel to his cause, Charlie Vickers's Sauron will have you rooting for the villain every step of the way. He brings a delightful sense of theatricality and purpose to every evil act, while the long-awaited introduction of Galadriel's MIA husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower, another major highlight of Season 3) finally provides the third point of the unlikeliest love triangle in the canon.

But if Sauron is the main driving force behind the best narrative arc of them all, "The Rings of Power" fares far worse everywhere else.

This "Lord of the Rings" series has always had trouble finding the right balance among its varying subplots, separated by narrative relevance and theme just as much as by distance. Nowhere does that feel more glaring than in Season 3. The courtly intrigue and succession struggles taking place in the Dwarven realm of Khazad-dûm aim for "House of the Dragon"-like dramatics, but neither of the plucky performances by Owain Arthur's King Durin or Sophia Nomvete's Queen Disa can make this feel like anything less than a misguided detour.

Similarly, the brewing civil war in Númenór takes ages to click into place (and, even then, not because of any established locals, but because Robert Aramayo's ever-conflicted Elf Elrond finally gets involved). And don't forget there's another B-plot entirely in the desert of Rhûn, with Daniel Weyman's Gandalf and Ciarán Hinds' Dark Wizard circling one another.

The further we get from Sauron's antics in Mordor, the less effective "The Rings of Power" undeniably becomes.

The five-year time jump should've allowed for J.D Payne, Patrick McKay, and co-writer Justin Doble to regroup strategically and reset the creative board a bit. And, to an extent, they do manage to cut things down to a more manageable size. A major character death or two helps trim an unwieldy ensemble that has only grown more so over the years, while others undergo some overdo changes in both personality and role. Even the lovable, pint-sized Harfoots have been written out completely this time around. But these are half-measures, at best. As this saga hits its midway point, viewers will be left with the impression that merely reshuffling the deck wasn't nearly enough.

These structural issues extend to the main conflict of Season 3, as well. In the early episodes, the creative team struggles with establishing the stakes of such an abstract threat as the One Ring. Season 1 had the (seemingly) unseen menace of Sauron working in its favor, while Season 2 organically built up to the epic siege of Eregion and the manipulation of Celebrimbor as its big emotional payoff. Season 3 pays lip service to the idea of Mordor's forces on the brink of total victory; but, other than a few minor skirmishes here and the aftermath of some battles there, we barely actually see this for ourselves.

It's a shame because, creatively and technically, the most expensive series on streaming has never looked better nor felt more cinematic. Directors Charlotte Brändström, Sanaa Hamri, and Stefan Schwartz depict a breathtaking level of scope and scale that modern viewers have almost become inured to these days. Together, J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay dream up some of the most spectacular fantasy concepts Tolkien nerds could only ever dare to imagine. As of the seven episodes out of eight made available for critics to review, it all builds up to the moment we've all been waiting for — one that, for a moment, absolutely lives up to the hype.

Is that enough? "Always is a long time," Galadriel suggests with a twinkle in her eye early on. With its five-season plan hopefully still in place, "The Rings of Power" doesn't have anywhere near that long to make up for lost time.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 premieres with four episodes November 11, 2026 on Prime Video.

The Blade Runner saga is set to continue amid the 2026 TV schedule, thanks to an upcoming limited series. Blade Runner 2099 presents the next chapter in this science-fiction-infused tale of humans and replicants and puts new protagonists at the forefront. Given what’s come before, it’s only natural to wonder whether the show has direct connections to Ridley Scott’s original 1982 film and Denis Villeneuve’s 2017 sequel, 2049. Well, the showrunner is now shedding some light on that front.

If it weren’t already clear due to the title, 2099 picks up fifty years after the events of the critically acclaimed Blade Runner 2049. That film left quite a few plot threads on the table, including the revelation that the late Eldon Tyrell gave replicants the ability to reproduce. Heading up the new show is Silka Luisa, who is a longtime fan of the franchise. Luisa recently spoke with SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend and was asked if events from 2049 would come into play. With that, she gave a very clear answer:

No, [Blade Runner 2049] is not directly connected to the show. What was an important early mandate was that audiences could come to the show not having seen the films, and this could stand alone. This could be an introduction to the world of Blade Runner, and it wouldn’t be dependent on you having watched 2049, you having watched the first Blade Runner. In that sense, we had to divorce ourselves from the narrative.

Why Edward James Olmos Says He Owes His Battlestar Galactica Legacy To Blade Runner

Some fans may be a tad disappointed to learn that replicant reproduction won’t be expanded upon during the events of the show. Yet Luisa’s “mandate” does indeed make a lot of sense. What she and her collaborators ultimately want is a show that fits snugly into the continuity but also doesn’t require watching the movies. (Of course, both of those films are excellent and deserve to be watched regardless.) In short, the Shining Girls creator is promising a series that works on its own, and that could do away with any trepidation newcomers may have about jumping in.

Blade Runner 2099 takes viewers to a Los Angeles that’s now fully controlled by replicants, and humans must essentially live within the lower levels of society. At the center of the story is Olwen, a Replicant Blade Runner (played by Michelle Yeoh) who is only days away from dying. She is eventually partnered with Marion Jessop to take on a case. However, unbeknownst to Olwen, “Marion” is actually a human named Cora (Hunter Schafer), who is only masquerading as a Replicant to achieve her own goals.

Per what’s been shared thus far, Yeoh and Schafer forged a strong bond on set not unlike Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling did while making 2049. However, as far as we know, Yeoh didn’t accidentally punch Schafer in the face like Ford did to Gosling. In fact, Yeoh was protective of her co-star amid production and, in a truly mom-coded move, she even bought Schafer a baby helmet.

The trailers for 2099 would suggest that such headgear was necessary, because a lot of intense moments have been teased thus far. Although fans won’t see any direct links to the Blade Runner films, Silka Luisa is aiming to dish out the action-infused thrills, heightened visuals and deep themes that have long permeated this franchise.

Check out Blade Runner 2099 when all eight episodes are released for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25. In the meantime, anyone who’s curious can stream the original movie for free on Pluto TV and check out 2049 on Prime as well.

#3536. In One Scene, Prime Video Officially Rewrites Gandalf’s Mission in Lord of the Rings

Gandalf isn’t just an old man, he’s a divine guardian

By the end of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 2, Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) had chosen his name and wizard staff and found a mentor in the enigmatic Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear). Season 3 picks up five years later, and Gandalf has spent that time vexing the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) and his forces in Rhûn. Gandalf sees the Dark Wizard as a dangerous foe, but their relationship is more complicated. Here’s what you need to know about the two wizards, and how they fit into J.R.R. Tolkien’s complex cosmology.

This article contains spoilers for the first three episodes of season 3 of The Rings of Power

Tolkien’s wizards aren’t just old men who wield magical power. They are Maiar, primordial spirits who serve the Valar, the divine beings that helped Eru Ilúvatar create the world. Sauron is a fallen Maia who served the rebel Vala Morgoth. The five Istari are Maiar sent in the form of old Men to Middle-earth to stop Sauron. They became known as wizards, and their members include Gandalf, Saruman, and Radagast.

Those are the only three wizards mentioned by name in The Lord of the Rings, but Tolkien’s Unfinished Tales mentions there were two more who were sent to the East: Pallando and Alatar. In season 3, episode 3, it’s revealed that the Dark Wizard is Pallando. He wanted more than to serve the Valar, so he killed Alatar, an act so evil it turned Rhûn into a desert. Pallando clearly has regrets as he’s trying to regrow the Tears of the Valar lilies that used to cover Rhûn. He hopes that he can make the land green again using one of Sauron’s rings.

“There’s a moment in the third episode, when Gandalf has infiltrated the Dark Wizard’s temple, and he sees Pallando sitting on the throne looking very forlorn,” series co-creator Patrick McKay told Polygon in a recent video interview. “That one shot, and that one moment from Ciarán Hinds, will lend a realism and a depth to that character that we as an audience were craving. Gandalf notices it, and I think the audience will notice it, too. Even in a story with all this magic and all this wonder, one good actor giving one good performance in one shot can speak volumes.”

The Dark Wizard’s servants fear Gandalf, who they say draws his power from the Secret Fire itself. Gandalf thinks that defeating the Dark Wizard is key to saving Middle-earth, since it will keep the armies of Rhûn from joining Sauron. Tom is skeptical that Gandalf is meant to defeat him, and the exasperated wizard leaves Tom’s hut to go catch a rabbit for stew. He then has a vision of the Secret Fire speaking to him, a moment McKay said is inspired by Moses and the Burning Bush.

The Secret Fire is the power that Eru Ilúvatar used to create the world, a force that burns within all sentient beings. Eru is Tolkien’s name for God, while the Secret Fire represents the Holy Spirit. When Gandalf faces the Balrog – a fallen Maia serving Morgoth – in Khazad-dûm in The Fellowship of the Ring, he shouts, "I am a servant of the Secret Fire.”

The Fire address Gandalf as Olórin, the name he was given as a Maiar before he came to Middle-earth and adopted the name Gandalf. It also calls him Mithrandir, his name among the Elves, which means the Grey Pilgrim. The Secret Fire then explains that Gandalf isn’t meant to defeat the Dark Wizard but to redeem him, because only together can they save Middle-earth.

Pallando needs the help. He hoped to get one of the nine rings for mortal men by sending emissaries to Sauron to accept his alliance with Rhûn. However, Sauron killed the most loyal of the Dark Wizard’s servants and encouraged the others to fight amongst themselves to claim a ring. Khamûl the Easterling (Zubin Varla) was the winner, and donning a ring freed him from the Dark Wizard’s flesh-warping curse. He returned to Rhûn a Nazgnagôl, challenging the Dark Wizard for his throne and ordering that he march his armies to Mordor. The Dark Wizard has effectively already been defeated, but if Gandalf can get him to see the light, they might be able to keep Sauron from getting even stronger.
